report:
## Evidence on Chlorhexidine-Alcohol vs. Iodine-Alcohol for Cesarean Skin Preparation

Your sister's view is supported by the strongest direct evidence available, though the overall picture has some nuance.

**The key trial:** Tuuli et al. (NEJM, 2016) conducted the largest randomized trial directly comparing chlorhexidine-alcohol (2% chlorhexidine gluconate + 70% isopropyl alcohol) against iodine-alcohol (8.3% povidone-iodine + 72.5% isopropyl alcohol) in 1,147 cesarean deliveries. Surgical-site infection (SSI) occurred in **4.0% of the chlorhexidine-alcohol group vs. 7.3% of the iodine-alcohol group** (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; p=0.02). This is the primary study driving the claim, and notably both arms were alcohol-based, isolating the active antiseptic as the variable.

**Corroborating meta-analyses:** A 2025 updated meta-analysis (Frontiers in Medicine) pooling eight RCTs found chlorhexidine-containing solutions superior to povidone-iodine for SSI prevention in cesarean delivery (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.54–0.89). A 2018 systematic review (PubMed) reached the same conclusion. A 2024 network meta-analysis (Journal of Hospital Infection) ranked alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine as having the highest probability of effectiveness, followed by alcohol-based povidone-iodine, though credible intervals overlapped—meaning the difference between the two alcohol-based agents was not definitively established across all analyses.

**A counterpoint:** The CAPICA trial (Springel et al., 2017) found no significant difference (6.3% vs. 7% SSI), but it compared chlorhexidine-alcohol against **aqueous** povidone-iodine (not iodine-alcohol), making it less directly relevant to your sister's specific claim.

**Bottom line:** The best direct evidence—Tuuli's large RCT—supports your sister's claim that chlorhexidine-alcohol reduces SSI compared with iodine-alcohol before cesarean delivery. Meta-analyses broadly favor chlorhexidine, though some analyses show overlapping confidence intervals, so the advantage is probable but not universally conclusive.
